sources.title: Clifford Edmund Bosworth: Karluk
sources.note: Encyclopaedia of Islam entry used for the overview and concise ending: federation size, titles, migrations, settlement, Islamization and continuing Karluk groups.

sources.title: History of Civilizations of Central Asia, volume III: The Türk Empire
sources.note: UNESCO scholarly chapter used for the 742 to 766 wars, westward movement, Talas and the establishment of Karluk power in Semirechye.

sources.title: Christopher Beckwith: The Tibetan Empire in Central Asia, excerpt
sources.note: Cambridge excerpt used narrowly for the Karluk role alongside Abbasid forces at the Battle of Talas in 751.

sources.title: OpenStax World History: East-West Interactions in the Early Middle Ages
sources.note: Peer-reviewed open textbook used to qualify the popular claim that Talas alone transferred papermaking westward.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Suyab
sources.note: Scholarly synthesis used for Suyab chronology, multicultural religious buildings, residential archaeology and later manuscript and inscription finds.

sources.title: International Institute for Central Asian Studies: Ak-Beshim report
sources.note: Institutional report page used for the excavation programme, geophysics, animal bone, seed and radiocarbon research at Ak-Beshim.

sources.title: Ak-Beshim 2019: Archaeological Research in the Chuy Valley
sources.note: University and Kyrgyz Academy field report used for late tenth- to early eleventh-century food remains, streets, possible toilets or wells and play objects, always date-labelled.

sources.title: Masashi Abe: Excavation at Ak-Beshim in the Chuy Valley
sources.note: Archaeological report used for late tenth-century ordinary houses, ovens, tools, spindle whorls and the abandonment shift toward Burana.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Central Asia, Economy before the Timurids
sources.note: Regional economic synthesis used with explicit scope labels for pastoral herds, agriculture, irrigation, felt work, household skills and Sogdian learning.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Sogdian Trade
sources.note: Scholarly synthesis used for the changing Sogdian caravan networks and traded goods in the Türk, Uyghur and Samanid eras.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Turko-Sogdian Coinage
sources.note: Numismatic synthesis used to distinguish earlier Sogdian-inscribed Türk issues from ninth- and tenth-century proto-Qarakhanid Arabic issues.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Ilak-Khanids
sources.note: Critical dynastic synthesis used for disputed Qarakhanid origins, Satuk Bughra Khan, conversion traditions and the conquests of 992 and 999.

sources.title: A Turkish Medical History Study on Qarluq Medicine in Tibetan Sources
sources.note: Modern study of later Tibetan medical historiography used only for a cautiously labelled Qarluq notice and the limits of reconstructing treatment.

sources.title: Talât Tekin: A Grammar of Orkhon Turkic
sources.note: Scholarly grammar supplies the Kül Tigin North 1 transliteration and translation naming the Karluk people.

sources.title: Unicode Standard: Old Turkic
sources.note: Technical standard used to identify the Old Turkic script and explain its right-to-left monumental writing direction.

sources.title: On the Author and Date of the Kül Tigin Inscription
sources.note: Scholarly article used for the 732 memorial context and the distinction between Turkic runiform sides and the Chinese face.

sources.title: UNESCO Tentative List: Silk Roads Sites in Kyrgyzstan
sources.note: UNESCO site description used for the archaeological character of Ak-Beshim and Burana and carefully dated later bath and water-main evidence.

sources.title: TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi: Karluklar
sources.note: Scholarly Turkish encyclopedia entry used for early federation, location, revolt and the sequence of alliances; claims are checked against other syntheses.

sources.title: The Cambridge History of Early Inner Asia, reading sample
sources.note: Cambridge scholarly volume excerpt used for the Karluk ruler’s changing titles and a dated Qarakhanid conversion sequence.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Central Asia in the Islamic Period up to the Mongols
sources.note: Regional synthesis used for Qarluq geography, Abbasid-period diplomacy and Islamization amid wider Transoxanian politics.

sources.title: The Qarakhanid World: Introduction
sources.note: Brill scholarly volume preserved by the Library of Congress used for the confederate background and uncertainty surrounding Qarakhanid formation.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Nomadism
sources.note: Regional reference used cautiously for mobile households, portable dwellings and gendered pastoral labor rather than as a Karluk household census.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Felt
sources.note: Material-culture reference used for Central Asian felt clothing, floor coverings, bags and horse equipment, with target-specific limits stated.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Sogdiana, History and Archaeology
sources.note: Regional archaeological synthesis used for inherited Sogdian settlement and irrigated cultivation rather than exclusive Karluk invention.

sources.title: Peter B. Golden: The Turk Imperial Tradition in the Pre-Chinggisid Era
sources.note: Scholarly historical study used for post-840 title claims and the continuing prestige of Türk imperial forms.

scopeNotes: New text needs independent review; earlier hashes do not certify it.

proposedOverrides.summary: A mobile federation built a Semirechye yabghu polity; it transformed amid Samanid pressure and disputed Qarakhanid formation while Karluk groups continued.

batchIdentityNotes: The exact imported id karluks is indexed circa 700 to 1000, with initial coverage intervals 700 to 800 and 900 to 1000 and no prior card.
The target is absent at 600, 800, 1000 and 1100. The missing 800 and 1000 snapshots conflict with the continuous index range and require explicit caveats.
The 700 shape is east of Suyab, Talas and Ili; the 900 shape reaches those places while neighboring Uyghur, Oghuz, Samanid and Tibetan features retain separate identities.
Western Türk, Göktürk, Türgesh factions, Uyghur, Oghuz, Samanid and Qarakhanid histories remain distinct. The atlas has no separate Türgesh id and spells its 1100 Qarakhanid successor karkhanids.
All coordinates, bounds, hashes and point tests describe imported display geometry only; none establishes modern borders, ethnicity, language or exclusive sovereignty.
